name: PRP (platelet-rich plasma) injections

lead: PRP is made by spinning your own blood to concentrate platelets, then injecting or applying it. In aesthetics it is used for fresher skin, fewer fine lines, brighter under-eyes and hair, and is often paired with microneedling as the 'vampire facial'. Under-eye hollows and dark circles are a common focus, often compared with hyaluronic acid tear-trough filler.

Platelets contain growth factors and cytokines thought to promote tissue repair, which is how treated skin is expected to look fresher. Most controlled trials are on knee osteoarthritis and other joint problems with mixed results, and facial studies are small case series.

paras: A blood draw is centrifuged in a clinic, and the plasma is injected with fine needles or mesotherapy devices, or applied after microneedling, usually as a short series of sessions. It is used on the face, under-eyes and scalp.

Adverse effects are low in most trials, but the CDC linked three HIV diagnoses in 2024 to an unlicensed spa reusing contaminated equipment for vampire facials. PRP itself is not FDA-regulated, so clinical use is off-label, while the preparation devices need clearance.

angle.text: PRP uses your own concentrated platelets, injected or applied with microneedling, for fresher skin, fewer fine lines and brighter under-eyes. The platelets' growth factors are thought to support tissue repair. Trial evidence is mostly from knee osteoarthritis rather than faces.

lead: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is a concentrate made from a person's own blood: a sample is spun in a centrifuge so that red cells are separated out and platelets are concentrated, typically to about three to five times their normal level in blood.[1] Platelets carry growth factors and signalling proteins, and the idea behind the treatment is that delivering them to a target area, by injection, by microneedling or with a mesotherapy device, prompts the tissue to repair and renew itself.[1] In appearance medicine that idea is applied to skin quality, under-eye hollows and thinning hair, which is how PRP reached looksmaxxing forums.[1][2]

In its best-known cosmetic form the plasma is applied to the face after microneedling, a combination marketed as the 'vampire facial'.[1][3] Proponents say the treatment stimulates collagen and new skin cells, giving smoother, brighter and firmer-looking skin; on looksmax.org the topic comes up in threads about tear-trough hollows, acne scars and 'biofillers', and about PRP as an alternative to hyaluronic acid filler.[2][4] The same concentrate is also injected into the scalp in hair-loss clinics.[1][5]

Most published research on PRP concerns joints and tendons, above all knee osteoarthritis, where randomized trials and meta-analyses have produced mixed results.[6][7][8][9] Research on the face is more limited and consists largely of small case series, while the scalp has the largest body of controlled data for any appearance use, with a 2023 meta-analysis pooling 27 trials in hair loss.[5] In the United States PRP itself is not regulated as a product, so clinical use is off-label, although the kits that prepare it are subject to FDA clearance.[1] A 2024 CDC-reported cluster of HIV infections tied to an unlicensed spa's vampire facials made the procedure's infection-control requirements a prominent news story.[1]

paras: PRP is also called autologous conditioned plasma. Preparation normally takes place in a clinic using commercial kits: blood is drawn, spun to separate its components and the platelet-rich layer is collected for use, with results that vary between people and facilities.[1] Wikipedia describes three broad categories defined by white-blood-cell and fibrin content: leukocyte-rich PRP, leukocyte-reduced PRP and leukocyte platelet-rich fibrin.[1] Platelets may be activated with thrombin or calcium chloride before use, though this step is described as optional because natural thrombin in the tissue can activate them after injection.[1]

The growth factors and cytokines associated with platelets include PDGF, TGF-beta, FGF, IGF-1 and IGF-2, VEGF and EGF, among others.[1] Studies of knee treatment have compared single-spin and double-spin preparation and examined how leukocyte concentration changes outcomes, which shows that preparation methods are not standardized.[10][11]

A related product, platelet-rich fibrin (PRF), is made by a similar spin without an anticoagulant and forms a gel-like matrix; looksmax.org posters discussing 'biofillers' are referring to PRF-type preparations. Dental researchers have studied PRF in periodontal defects, including a 2024 network meta-analysis.[4][12]

According to Wikipedia, the term 'platelet-rich plasma' was first used by Kingsley in 1954; the first PRP blood banks appeared in the 1960s and the technique spread in the 1970s, initially in hematology for patients with low platelet counts.[1] Use extended to maxillofacial surgery in the 1980s, and Wikipedia credits a 1987 open-heart operation in Italy (Ferrari and colleagues) as an early surgical use.[1] A 1998 randomized trial in oral surgery examined PRP as a growth-factor enhancement for bone grafts.[13]

PRP drew public attention between roughly 2009 and 2011 because of its use by professional athletes for tendon and muscle injuries, covered by outlets including the New York Times and Scientific American.[1] In January 2011 the World Anti-Doping Agency removed intramuscular PRP from its prohibited list, citing lack of evidence that it enhances performance.[1] PRP began to be considered for androgenetic alopecia and alopecia areata around 2006.[1]

The cosmetic 'vampire facial' reached a mass audience in 2013, when Kim Kardashian West posted an Instagram photograph of her blood-covered face during the procedure; she later said she regretted it.[3] Interest in injecting a person's own blood goes back further: autohemotherapy was a popular dermatology treatment in the early twentieth century before being abandoned, with interest returning in the 2000s.[3]

PRP has been used or investigated for tendon and joint problems, hair loss, chronic wounds, assisted reproduction and aesthetic medicine.[1] Registered studies include PRP for knee osteoarthritis (a completed 153-person study),[14] vocal fold atrophy, rotator cuff syndrome, internal disc disruption and chronic non-healing wounds.[15][16][17]

In aesthetic practice PRP is injected into the face, applied after microneedling, or delivered with a mesotherapy device, with the aim of improving texture, fine lines, tone and the look of tired skin.[1] Wikipedia notes that the supporting claims for aesthetic PRP are largely promotional.[1] Reported side effects of a vampire facial include redness, swelling, bruising and tingling; providers quote about two days of recovery, although some patients report a week or more with scabbing.[3]

Within looksmaxxing communities the face-related interest centres on tear-trough hollows and dark under-eye circles, where posters weigh PRP against hyaluronic acid filler priced similarly, and on skin texture and acne scarring.[2][4] One 2026 case series of ten patients with mild-to-moderate photoaging gave three monthly PRP treatments and reported thicker dermis on high-frequency ultrasound, improved pores, wrinkles and pigmentation on a skin analyzer, and transient redness as the main side effect. A 2021 report of seven patients described PRP mesotherapy for corticosteroid-induced rosacea-like dermatitis.

Clinics offer PRP scalp injections as an add-on or alternative to minoxidil or finasteride, typically as a series of monthly sessions followed by maintenance treatments every few months, according to Wikipedia; its authors say efficacy depends on the number of sessions, preparation method, age, sex and injection site.[1] Reported changes are in hair density and shaft thickness rather than in the pattern of hair loss itself.[1][5]

Microneedling creates tiny channels in the skin and is often paired with topical or injected products. A 2022 meta-analysis of 12 studies (459 patients) on melasma found that microneedling added to topical treatments, which included tranexamic acid, vitamin C, PRP and depigmenting agents, produced additional improvement and was well tolerated.[6] That analysis examined microneedling as an adjunct across several topicals, not PRP alone.

Hair is the appearance area with the most controlled data. A 2015 randomized, evaluator-blinded, placebo-controlled half-head trial in 23 people with pattern hair loss (20 analysed) injected PRP into one half of the scalp and placebo into the other, three times at 30-day intervals, and followed participants for two years. Mean hair count in the target area rose by 33.6 and total hair density by 45.9 hairs per cm2 against baseline; biopsies showed thicker epidermis and more follicles, no side effects were reported during treatment, and four patients reported progressive hair loss again by 16 months and were re-treated. The authors concluded that PRP may be a safe and effective option and called for larger controlled studies.[18]

A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis pooled 27 controlled trials (1,117 participants): 18 in androgenetic alopecia and 9 in alopecia areata, 11 using a split-head design. Compared with saline injections, PRP increased hair density over medium-term follow-up (mean difference 25.6 hairs per cm2, 95% CI 2.62 to 48.57), but the authors rated the evidence low in quality, noted wide variation in PRP types and schedules, and reported no serious adverse events related to PRP.[5]

For facial appearance the literature is smaller: the 2026 photoaging case series of ten patients and the seven-patient rosacea-like dermatitis report are uncontrolled. No randomized trial of PRP for under-eye hollows or dark circles has been identified.

Most of the large human trials concern the knee. A 2021 meta-analysis of randomized trials compared PRP with hyaluronic acid injections for knee osteoarthritis.[7] A 2015 randomized trial reported no superiority of PRP over viscosupplementation,[8] whereas a 2017 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 162 patients reported that three PRP injections outperformed a single injection and hyaluronic acid in early osteoarthritis.[19] A 2017 meta-analysis of randomized trials examined efficacy,[9] and a 2021 meta-analysis of eight studies (648 patients) found PRP better than corticosteroid injection for symptoms at 3, 6 and 9 months.[20] The 2021 RESTORE randomized trial in JAMA compared PRP with placebo for pain and medial tibial cartilage volume in knee osteoarthritis; its introduction noted that most guidelines had not recommended PRP for the knee because of lack of high-quality evidence.[21] A 2024 ESSKA-ICRS consensus statement set out recommendations for different clinical scenarios.[22]

For tendons, a 2021 meta-analysis of eight randomized trials examined PRP for rotator cuff tendinopathy,[23] and a 2025 meta-analysis of 27 randomized trials (1,779 patients) compared PRP with corticosteroid injection across rotator cuff, tennis elbow, plantar fasciitis and tenosynovitis.[24] Other randomized trials have tested PRP in lumbar disc disease, ankle osteoarthritis and COVID-19-related olfactory loss.[25][26][27] A systematic review has also examined PRP for temporomandibular joint osteoarthritis.[28]

Wikipedia summarises the overall picture as mixed: tentative support for knee osteoarthritis, mixed results for rotator cuff disease, a 2021 Cochrane review finding no good evidence for elbow tendinitis, and positive 2024 meta-analyses for venous and diabetic foot ulcers.[1]

Wikipedia reports that adverse effects are low in most trials and that a Cochrane review found weak evidence of harm at comparable low rates in treated and untreated people.[1] Because the material comes from the patient's own blood, allergic or immune reactions are not the usual concern; the main risk is infection when equipment or technique is not sterile.[1][3]

In September 2018 the New Mexico Department of Health warned that at least one spa offering vampire facials could potentially spread HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C.[3] In April 2024 the CDC reported that three women diagnosed with HIV had received such facials at an unlicensed Albuquerque spa where the operator reused blood-contaminated single-use equipment without sterilization; about 200 other former clients tested negative.[1][3]

The FDA does not regulate PRP itself, because it is exempt from the traditional pathways as a human tissue and blood product, so its clinical use is off-label; the devices used to prepare it are subject to FDA clearance.[1]

On looksmax.org, PRP appears mainly in threads about the under-eye area and skin quality. A poster asked whether PRP gave better results than simple tear-trough filler for about the same price, and replies raised concern that non-dissolving filler can leave pocket-like bags and that injection directly in the tear trough carries complication risk.[2] Another member described a clinic build-out for vampire facials and platelet-rich fibrin 'biofillers' for the tear trough, chin and jaw, which drew jokes and offers to book appointments from other users.[4]

Outside appearance forums, PRP appears in strength-training and sports communities, where lifters and fans discuss it for injuries; for example a 2014 T Nation thread speculated that an NFL player would have access to PRP injections.[29] For lifters, faster recovery of joints and tendons is discussed as a way to keep training and building physique.

lore.intro: Looksmaxxing communities discuss PRP mainly as a skin and under-eye treatment, often next to filler, microneedling and 'biofillers'; some members describe plans to perform the procedures themselves or in their own clinics.[2][4]
